Data: [TidyTuesday 2026-09-29](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-09-29).

The Joint Research Centre of the European Commission describes more than 11,000 urban centres worldwide.
For health, it counts the hospitals and pharmacies found inside each one in 2024, and the share of people who live within 1 km of one.
Those facilities come from open map data, so a count is what someone mapped, not what exists.

Taken at face value, the French numbers say something odd.
Lille has 148 pharmacies for about 907,000 people, or 16.3 per 100,000.
Paris has 210 for 9.3 million, or 2.3 per 100,000.
That makes Lille seven times better served than Paris, with 60% of its people near a pharmacy against 23% in Paris.

Anyone who has walked through Paris knows that is not true.
France had 20,242 pharmacies on 1 January 2025, according to the Ordre national des pharmaciens.
That is about 29.5 for every 100,000 people, and every city in the figure falls well short of it.
Across the 68 French urban centres that have a count, the map finds only 1,004 pharmacies for 22.8 million people.

So the ranking measures the map, not the pharmacies.
Lille and Bordeaux look well served because their pharmacies were mapped more fully than elsewhere.
Paris looks like a desert because most of its pharmacies were not mapped.
The hatched part of each row is the gap between what the map shows and the national rate.

Some cautions.
The national rate is a yardstick, not a target for each city, since pharmacies in France are spread by the population of each commune and are not concentrated in cities.
A city here is the urban centre defined by the Degree of Urbanisation, which can be larger or smaller than the commune with the same name.
The 20 cities are the largest French urban centres by population in 2025.
